newsitem.title: USA: Mass.officials clash on auto-health insurance link.
newsitem.headline: Mass.officials clash on auto-health insurance link.

text.p: Politicians, insurance executives and lawyers clashed on Premier Insurance Co's plan to offer its Massachusetts policyholders discounts if they choose to be treated in Premier's health network after an auto accident, State House News reported.

Premier's plan was approved by state Insurance Commissioner Linda Ruthardt last year, but she withdrew her endorsement when the state Academy of Trial Lawyers sued on grounds that the issue had not been given a public hearing.

When it did have a public hearing last August, Sen. Dianne Wilkerson (D-Roxbury), co-chairwoman of the state legislature's Insurance Committee, told Ruthardt that such a program needs legislative approval.
The committee heard a bill on Monday that would require Ruthardt to delay approving programs like Premier's until the legislature has fully investigated them.

Edwin Rinehiner, president and chief executive officer of Worcester-based Premier, told the hearing, "Every time we try to do something to contain costs, we're stopped by somebody who wants to get their hand in that $3 billion cookie jar."

Rinehiner and Jim Harrington of the American Insurers Association said lawyers and chiropractors have an interest in making sure personal injury medical costs surpass $2,000 per claim, because that is the threshold costs must exceed before a lawsuit can be filed.
Managed care, Rinehiner said, helps keep costs down. He downplayed the possibility that doctors in Premier's network would try to keep costs low in order cut down on litigation.
Policyholders who opt not to use the Premier health network are not penalized, he said. He estimated that just 15 percent of Premier's policyholders are enrolled in the program.
